courseTitle: The ABA problem and tagged pointers
lessonTitle: Tagged pointers: a version counter beside the pointer
md: Tagged pointer = pointer plus a counter compared and swapped as one unit, bumped on every successful CAS. It turns "same value" into "same value and same version".

courseTitle: Ablation studies: what each pipeline stage really adds
lessonTitle: Per-query deltas, paired tests and confidence intervals
md: Queries are not the only noise source. If a stage is trained, its score also varies with the random seed. Use the same seeds and checkpoints for every stage you are not ablating, and when the ablated stage itself is retrained, run several seeds and report the spread, or a seed-to-seed swing can masquerade as a component effect.

courseTitle: Broken access control and authorization design
lessonTitle: Sequential vs random ids, and why random ids are not authorization
md: Parler's public posts were meant to be readable one at a time. Sequential ids plus no rate limit turned "anyone can read a post" into "anyone can copy the entire site, with GPS locations". Authorization decides who may read an object; rate limits and unpredictable ids decide how cheaply someone can read all of them. You need both.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: What Active Directory is: one directory for thousands of machines
md: A domain is not a wall. Domains in one forest trust each other automatically, and the Enterprise Admins group of the forest root is an administrator in every domain (next lesson). Plan protection for the whole forest, not one domain at a time.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: AS-REP roasting and password spraying against AD
md: Turning off pre-authentication hands out crackable material to anyone; 4768 with pre-auth type 0 finds it. Spraying hides under per-account lockout; count distinct accounts per source in 4771 and 4776, not failures per account.

courseTitle: Active Directory and Kerberos attacks
lessonTitle: Tiered administration, Protected Users and LAPS
md: Tiering fails quietly through agents. A backup, monitoring or patching tool that runs as SYSTEM on DCs, managed from a Tier 1 console, makes that console Tier 0. List everything installed on DCs and everyone who controls it.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: PDF: objects, filters, automatic actions and JavaScript
md: Do not open a suspicious PDF in your everyday reader to 'see what it says'. Readers run JavaScript and follow actions; that is the point of the file. Triage with pdfid and parse with pdf-parser, which only read bytes.

courseTitle: Advanced malware analysis: maldocs, scripts, unpacking, anti-analysis
lessonTitle: Ransomware crypto mistakes: how Hive's files were decrypted
md: Crypto flaws in ransomware are rare, and once published they can be fixed in the next version. Plan recovery around offline backups; treat a decryptor as a lucky bonus, and get one only from a trusted source.

courseTitle: Advanced memory exploitation concepts: ROP, heap and kernel
lessonTitle: What this means for engineers: safe languages, fuzzing, defaults
md: Prevent, then detect, then mitigate. Memory-safe languages remove bug classes; sanitizers and fuzzing catch what remains; mitigations on by default raise the cost of what slips through; and fast patching shortens the window. Every rung an attacker must climb is one you can remove.

courseTitle: Adversary emulation, red teaming and purple teaming
lessonTitle: Scoring outcomes and measuring detection coverage
md: Averages hide shapes. An average score of 3 can be every technique alerting but never triaged, or half the techniques perfect and half invisible. Always report the distribution and the gap categories with the average, and never report coverage as "techniques with a rule tagged".

courseTitle: Agent benchmarks: SWE-bench, tau-bench and reading the scores
lessonTitle: tau-bench: simulated users, database state and pass^k
md: The paper calls r = 1 necessary but not sufficient: an agent that issues the correct return *without* asking for confirmation still scores 1, even though it broke policy. Database comparison catches wrong outcomes, not bad conduct along the way.

courseTitle: Agent harnesses: the loop, tools, context and control around an LLM
lessonTitle: Permissions, traces and evaluation
md: Permission checks are only as strong as the sandbox behind them. Anthropic recommends extensive testing in sandboxed environments for agents; run untrusted or autonomous agents in a container or VM with limited network and credentials, and reserve modes that skip approval for those isolated environments.

courseTitle: Agent verification: checking an agent's work before you trust it
lessonTitle: Why an agent saying done is not evidence of done
md: Misconception: if the agent ran the tests itself and reported success, the work is verified. The report is model output, and tests the agent wrote or could edit are not independent. Run the checks in the harness, on a clean copy, with tests the agent did not control.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: How an LLM app is built: one stream of tokens
md: An LLM app has one channel. Instructions and data are both tokens in the context window, and the model, not your code, decides what each token means.

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Approval gates and egress allowlists
md: Gate side effects with a real, informed human decision. Constrain network egress to exact hosts in code the model cannot influence. Together they turn "the model was fooled" into "the model asked and was refused".

courseTitle: AI and LLM security: prompt injection, agents and model risks
lessonTitle: Defence in layers: privilege separation, provenance and egress
md: Design so that a fully hijacked model still cannot do harm: it cannot reach what it should not read, cannot act without a check it cannot talk past, and cannot send data anywhere you did not list.

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: Why AI text needs a planted signal
md: A text watermark is a keyed, pseudorandom preference applied at sampling time. Detection re-derives the preference from the text and asks whether the text agrees with it far more often than chance.

courseTitle: Watermarking AI outputs
lessonTitle: Attacks on text watermarks: edits, paraphrase, spoofing and stealing
md: Text watermarks fail in four ways: edits that re-randomize the seeds, meaning-preserving rewrites, spoofing that plants the signal in text the provider never wrote, and stealing by learning the pattern. Treat a positive detection as statistical evidence about origin, not proof of authorship, and a negative one as no information.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Why the mean and standard deviation hide outliers
md: A score is only as good as its model of normal. Mean and standard deviation break under masking; median and MAD fix that for one variable. For data with clusters and local structure you need scores that look at the joint shape of the data, which is what the next lessons build.

courseTitle: Anomaly and outlier detection
lessonTitle: Evaluating detectors when 1 percent of points are anomalies
md: Under heavy imbalance, judge detectors by ranking quality where you will act: AP and the PR curve for the whole ranking, precision@k for the review budget. ROC-AUC hides false alarms because it divides them by the huge number of normal points.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: The authorization code flow with PKCE, step by step
md: The code travels through the browser, so assume it can leak. PKCE ties redeeming it to a secret that never left the client that started the flow.

courseTitle: API security, OAuth and JWT
lessonTitle: Classic JWT bugs: alg none, RS256 to HS256, kid and jku
md: Every one of these bugs is the same mistake: letting data inside the unverified token decide how the token is verified. The receiver fixes the algorithm, the key set and the audience; the token only gets to say which of the receiver's keys it used.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Design review in the cycle: deciding which changes get a threat model
md: A design review that happens after the code is written is an audit, not a design review. If the triage questionnaire lives in the pull request template instead of the design template, the expensive decisions (which vendor, where the data lives) are already made.

courseTitle: Secure SDLC, code review and vulnerability management
lessonTitle: Security champions, bug bounties and disclosure programmes
md: Champions scale security inside; a VDP with safe harbour invites help from outside. Both fail without the basics: someone answers the reports, and fixes have owners and deadlines.

courseTitle: Crash recovery (ARIES)
lessonTitle: Why a crash needs both undo and redo
md: Steal creates the need for **undo**, no-force creates the need for **redo**. ARIES allows both, so it must do both, using only the log and a little state stored on each page.

courseTitle: Asymmetric embeddings: query vs document input types
lessonTitle: Four ways to tell the model which side a text is on
md: All four designs encode the same idea: one shared vector space, two roles. Use the exact pair (prefixes, instructions or input types) that the model was trained with, on the side it was trained for.

courseTitle: Calling LLM APIs at scale: concurrency, rate limits, retries, caching
lessonTitle: Batch jobs, idempotent pipelines and putting it together
md: Order of checks for each call: cache first (free, instant), then dedupe in-flight duplicates, then a concurrency limit and a rate limiter, then the API with bounded jittered retries. Anything that is not latency-sensitive goes to a batch job. Every side effect is keyed so that re-running the job is safe.

courseTitle: Atomics and compare-and-swap (CAS)
lessonTitle: Compare-and-swap: write only if nothing changed, else retry
md: CAS turns "read, compute, write" into "read, compute, write *only if what I read is still there*". The retry loop is the general recipe: load, compute from the loaded value, CAS, and on failure recompute from the value CAS returned.

courseTitle: Audio embeddings and classification
lessonTitle: Zero-shot classification with CLAP audio and text embeddings
md: Choosing an approach: use a pretrained tagger's scores directly when AudioSet classes cover your needs; train a small head on frozen embeddings when you have a few hundred labeled clips; fine-tune when you have more data and compute; use CLAP-style zero-shot when labels change often or you have no labeled audio, and expect lower accuracy than a supervised head on the same classes.

courseTitle: Authentication and identity attacks
lessonTitle: Online attacks: brute force, credential stuffing, password spraying
md: Brute force is one account, many passwords. Credential stuffing is many leaked pairs. Spraying is one password, many accounts. MFA and breached-password checks defeat all three; detection needs counts across accounts, not just per account.

courseTitle: Autonomous research agents: plan, search, verify, evaluate
lessonTitle: Why research needs a loop, not one retrieval
md: A research agent is not a bigger retrieval call. It is a harness loop whose next query depends on what the last read revealed, and whose output is a set of claims each tied to a source.

courseTitle: Amazon Bedrock and the AWS generative AI stack
lessonTitle: On-demand capacity: tokens per minute and the max_tokens trap
md: Set `max_tokens` close to the longest answer you really need. The AWS docs say it directly: if you hit TPM quotas earlier than expected, reduce max_tokens to better approximate your completions. Measure real output lengths from the `OutputTokenCount` metric that Bedrock publishes to CloudWatch, the AWS monitoring service.

courseTitle: Binary reverse engineering: ARM64, compiled languages and firmware
lessonTitle: Firmware images: layout, signatures and entropy
md: Everything here uses an image we built from our own code. Real vendor firmware is often covered by licence terms, and some contains other parties' secrets; analyse only devices and images you own or are authorised to test, and never download firmware to attack devices you do not control.

courseTitle: 1.58-bit LLMs: ternary weights, BitLinear and bitnet.cpp
lessonTitle: Running ternary models fast: I2_S, lookup tables, real numbers
md: Loading the 2B4T checkpoint in Hugging Face `transformers` (the standard Python model library) saves memory but gives no speed or energy gain; the model card says the efficiency needs the dedicated bitnet.cpp kernels.

courseTitle: B-trees vs LSM-trees and compaction
lessonTitle: B+trees update in place, and random writes pay for it
md: A B+tree's write cost is set by the **page**, not the row: a random small update rewrites a whole page at a random location. Reads are cheap because each key lives in exactly one place.

courseTitle: Buffer pools and page eviction: CLOCK, LRU-K and 2Q
lessonTitle: The buffer pool: frames, a page table, pins and dirty pages
md: A buffer pool is a write-back page cache owned by the database. On a miss it must evict some *unpinned* page, and write it out first if it is *dirty*. Everything else in this course is about choosing that page well.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Business impact analysis: from processes to tolerable downtime
md: A BIA turns "everything is critical" into an ordered list: for each process, the impact over time, the resources it needs, and its maximum tolerable downtime, decided by the people who own the loss. Everything later (targets, backups, sites, tests) is sized from it.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Restoring at the right size: Atlassian's two-week outage, April 2022
md: Prevent mass deletion at the API (typed IDs, previews, batch caps, second approvers), make deletion reversible for a period (soft delete), and practise restores at the sizes you will really need. Atlassian met its RPO and still took up to 14 days, because its restore procedure did not fit the shape of the loss.

courseTitle: Resilience, business continuity and disaster recovery
lessonTitle: Crisis management: decisions, workarounds and communication
md: Crisis management decides and speaks; recovery teams fix. Keep a decision log, a fixed update rhythm, one authorised voice, contact lists stored outside production, and manual workarounds written down before they are needed.

courseTitle: Tokenizer-free and byte-level models
lessonTitle: Entropy patching: spend compute where the next byte is hard
md: Entropy patching spends a global step where the next byte is hard to predict and lets cheap local layers handle predictable runs. The threshold sets the average patch size, and therefore the compute.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: Why C memory bugs compile cleanly and ship
md: C's type system cannot express *who owns this block* or *how long this pointer is valid*. Rust's ownership and borrow rules are exactly that missing information, checked at compile time.

courseTitle: C and Rust: from malloc and free to ownership and unsafe
lessonTitle: Build a safe type on unsafe: a minimal Vec from scratch
md: MyVec is a teaching subset. It rejects zero-sized types, has no insert, remove, iterators or slice access, and does not handle a panic in the middle of an operation. The Rustonomicon's later Vec chapters add each of these, which is a measure of how much care std's Vec holds.

courseTitle: Cache hierarchy (L1/L2/L3) and cache lines
lessonTitle: The working-set staircase and average access time
md: Think in **miss rate**, not hit rate. CMU's point: 99% hits is twice as fast as 97% when misses cost 100 cycles, because the misses dominate the time.

courseTitle: Circuit tracing and attribution graphs
lessonTitle: Validating a graph with interventions
md: Graph first, intervention second. The graph proposes which features matter and how; perturbing those features in the real model is what turns a picture into evidence. Expect directional agreement, not exact numbers.

courseTitle: Click models and unbiased learning to rank
lessonTitle: Inverse propensity scoring turns clicks into unbiased labels
md: IPS fixes the examination part of the bias, not click noise. If users sometimes click irrelevant results, those clicks are also upweighted. Joachims et al. show that, as long as relevant results are clicked more often than irrelevant ones, this bias is order preserving: with enough data the best ranking stays the same, but the estimates are no longer exactly relevance.

courseTitle: XSS, CSRF and client-side attacks
lessonTitle: When users need HTML: sanitising with DOMPurify
md: Sanitise as the **last step before insertion**, in the context where it will be used. Sanitising on the server and then running the result through an emoji or link replacer in the browser re-opens the TweetDeck kind of bug: new HTML created after the check, never checked.

courseTitle: CLIP and image embeddings: learning vision from captions
lessonTitle: Zero-shot classification with prompts, probes and robustness
md: Robustness does not survive adapting CLIP to ImageNet. Fitting a logistic-regression classifier on CLIP features with ImageNet labels raised ImageNet accuracy by 9.2% to 85.4%, yet average accuracy across the shifted datasets slightly decreased. Gains on the training distribution and robustness are different things.

courseTitle: Cloud detection and incident response
lessonTitle: SCARLETEEL 2023: from a Kubernetes pod to the AWS account
md: SCARLETEEL crossed three evidence domains: the container (runtime telemetry), the cloud control plane (CloudTrail) and a second account (its own CloudTrail). Data events were off and some logging was disabled, so the investigators could only say the attacker "went through the buckets", not exactly what they read.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: Landing zones: an account layout that contains failure
md: Common mistake: "our security tooling runs in the management account because it can see everything there." That puts your most targeted tools in the one account no SCP protects. Delegate administration to a Security Tooling account and keep the management account for organization tasks only.

courseTitle: Cloud security architecture: guardrails, serverless, attack paths
lessonTitle: Google Cloud in depth: service accounts, actAs and impersonation
md: Google Cloud escalation runs through service accounts: actAs is PassRole and Token Creator is AssumeRole. Remove Editor from default service accounts, grant both roles on individual service accounts only, and never attach a privileged service account to compute that less trusted code can run on.

courseTitle: Cloud security and IAM
lessonTitle: Instance roles at scale: IMDSv2 everywhere and a data perimeter
md: Roll a perimeter policy out carefully. Because `aws:SourceVpc` exists only for requests through VPC endpoints, any instance role that calls an AWS service over the public internet will start failing. Test in one account first, and check which services each workload calls.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: Lloyd's algorithm by hand, and why the seeds decide
md: k-means++ is the only step here with a guarantee. Arthur and Vassilvitskii prove $E[\phi] \le 8(\ln k + 2)\,\phi_{OPT}$ after seeding alone, before a single Lloyd iteration; the iterations can then only lower it. In scikit-learn `init="k-means++"` is the default (a greedy variant that tries several candidates per step), and `n_init="auto"` means 1 run with k-means++ but 10 runs with `init="random"`.

courseTitle: Clustering: k-means, DBSCAN and finding failure patterns
lessonTitle: Evaluating a clustering with and without labels
md: Stability rewards a repeatable answer, not a correct one. With enough restarts k-means finds the k = 2 global optimum every time, so it is perfectly stable, and that optimum is the one that scores ARI 0.41 against the truth. Instability is a useful alarm; stability is not a certificate. Report it next to coverage and, where you have them, labels.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: What -O0, -O2 and -O3 actually switch on
md: An -O level is a bundle of passes. -O0 keeps every variable in memory for debuggability; -O2 is the standard speed level; -O3, -Os, -Og and -Ofast each trade something (size, speed, debuggability, strictness) for something else.

courseTitle: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
lessonTitle: LTO and ThinLTO: optimizing across source files
md: LTO can expose latent bugs. Code with undefined behavior, or with mismatched declarations of the same function in different files, may have "worked" only because the optimizer could not see across files. When LTO breaks a program, suspect the program first; lesson 5 shows how optimizers exploit UB.

courseTitle: Computer-use agents: seeing screens and driving mouse and keyboard
lessonTitle: The observe-act loop: screenshots in, mouse and keyboard out
md: Misconception: the model "sees" the screen continuously. It sees only the screenshots you return, at the moments you return them. If a dialog pops up after your capture, the model does not know about it until the next screenshot.

courseTitle: Concurrency testing with loom and ThreadSanitizer
lessonTitle: How loom takes over the scheduler and walks every schedule
md: Every source of non-determinism must come from loom: no real time, randomness or I/O inside `loom::model`. Determinism is what lets loom replay a schedule and flip one choice at a time.

courseTitle: Consistency models: from linearizable to eventual
lessonTitle: What a consistency model promises, and why replicas break it
md: Model A is **stronger** than model B when every history A allows is also allowed by B (A is a subset of B). Stronger models rule out more surprising results, and usually cost more coordination, latency or availability.

courseTitle: Consistent hashing and hot-key mitigation
lessonTitle: Hot keys: perfect key balance, unbalanced traffic
md: Consistent hashing balances keys. Hot keys need a different tool: copies (replication, client caches) for read-hot keys, splitting for write-hot keys, and miss coalescing for keys that expire under load.

courseTitle: Constraint satisfaction solvers: backtracking, AC-3, CDCL and CP-SAT
lessonTitle: Backtracking search with forward checking and MRV
md: Choose the **variable** that is most likely to fail, and the **value** that is most likely to succeed. Every variable must be assigned eventually, so failing early on the hardest one costs nothing and prunes the most. But only one solution is needed, so values should keep the most options open.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: What ships in an image: base images, distroless and scanning
md: Misconception: "we scan, so our images are safe". A scanner only knows published vulnerabilities in recognised packages. It does not find your own code's bugs, a backdoored but unlisted dependency, or a secret left in a layer unless a secret scanner runs too.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: RBAC: roles, bindings and the permissions that escalate
md: Misconception: "they can only create pods, not read Secrets". Pod creation lets them mount any Secret in the namespace into a pod they control and read it from inside. Treat create-pods as read-all-secrets for that namespace, unless admission policy restricts what pods may mount.

courseTitle: Container and Kubernetes security
lessonTitle: Secrets: base64 is not encryption
md: Misconception: "our Secrets are encrypted because they look scrambled in kubectl". That is base64. Check whether the API server has --encryption-provider-config at all, and whether identity is first; the docs list both as signs that encryption at rest is not enabled.

courseTitle: Containers and Kubernetes: namespaces, cgroups and scheduling
lessonTitle: What an image actually is: layers, unions and digests
md: An image is an ordered list of content-addressed changesets plus a config. Everything else follows from that one sentence: identical layers are stored and transferred once, a deletion only adds a marker, and changing any layer invalidates every layer after it. Order your build steps from least to most frequently changing.

courseTitle: Conversational query refinement: tracking search state across turns
lessonTitle: Resolving the second one and those against what was shown
md: References point at a response, not at the conversation. Store the ordered ids you displayed, with a version, and resolve ordinals, attributes and *those* against that stored list.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Hidden computation: filler tokens, encoded reasoning, paraphrasing
md: A CoT can carry reasoning a reader misses in two ways: computation in activations at token positions (filler) and information in choices a reader ignores (encoding). Neither has been seen in current models on the tasks tested, both can be trained in, and paraphrasing by a weaker model limits the second to a few bits per answer.

courseTitle: Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitorability
lessonTitle: Why CoT is monitorable at all, and how to keep it so
md: CoT monitoring is most trustworthy where the CoT is necessary: behaviors that need long serial reasoning must pass through readable tokens. It is weakest for behaviors a model can do in one forward pass, and it stays useful only as long as training does not teach the CoT to look clean.

courseTitle: Cross-encoder rerankers: scoring query and document together
lessonTitle: Inside the forward pass: query and document attend to each other
md: Joint attention makes each document token's representation a function of the query. That is the source of the accuracy gain and the reason nothing beyond tokenization can be reused across queries.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: The one-time pad: perfect secrecy and the cost of reusing a key
md: Any cipher that XORs a keystream onto data must never produce the same keystream twice. Remember this; it returns in lessons 6, 7 and 15 under the names counter reuse, nonce reuse and ECDSA nonce reuse.

courseTitle: Cryptography for engineers: primitives and how they fail
lessonTitle: Putting it together: TLS 1.3 and the rules of using crypto
md: Most cryptographic failures in the wild are not broken maths. They are reused nonces, weak randomness, unchecked parameters, outdated algorithms and home-made constructions. Security review of crypto code is mostly checking these nine rules.

courseTitle: Using cryptography safely: how real systems got it wrong
lessonTitle: Secret-dependent timing: comparisons, Minerva and TPM-Fail
md: Any secret that influences control flow, memory addresses or loop lengths can leak through time, over a network or from another process. Use library functions built to be constant time, keep crypto libraries and firmware patched, and never write your own comparison or scalar multiplication.

courseTitle: CUTLASS and CuTe: tiling GEMMs across the GPU memory hierarchy
lessonTitle: CuTe layouts: shape and stride as an index function
md: A layout is just a function: coordinate in, integer offset out, computed as an inner product with the strides. Everything else in CuTe (tiling, partitioning across threads, MMA operand maps) is built by combining such functions.

courseTitle: CXL and memory disaggregation: far memory you can load and store
lessonTitle: Why servers strand DRAM and why DDR alone cannot fix it
md: CXL attacks two problems at once: capacity and bandwidth that DDR pins cannot scale (memory *expansion*), and DRAM that is stuck on the wrong host (memory *pooling*). Both rely on one property: the CPU reaches the memory with plain loads and stores, so applications do not change.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Three questions before you touch a system: law, permission, ethics
md: Ask three questions every time: is it legal (law), is it authorised (the owner, in writing, in scope), is it right (harm to others). Keep evidence of each answer before you start.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Crossing borders: the Budapest Convention and jurisdiction
md: Testing a system abroad from home does not put you under only your own country's law. Both CMA section 5 and CyBOK's analysis point the same way: the target's location can be enough.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Monitoring, interception and privacy law in security work
md: Login banners are not magic. They support consent and notice, but they do not authorise intercepting people who never saw them (a visitor on guest Wi-Fi, the other party to an email), and they do not override necessity and retention limits.

courseTitle: Cyber law, ethics and the security researcher
lessonTitle: Putting it together: a researcher's decision checklist
md: Every lesson's cases share one pattern: the person in trouble had a story that made sense to them ('it was public', 'they agreed afterwards', 'it's only code', 'nothing was merged'). The checklist exists because your own story is the hardest one to see past.

courseTitle: Data mixing and curation: how DoReMi learns the pretraining mixture
lessonTitle: Mixtures that change during training: annealing data and mid-training
md: A gain from an anneal is not proof that the data would help as much over a full pretraining run, or at a larger scale. Llama 3's math annealing helped the 8B model a lot and the 405B model hardly at all. Use anneals to rank candidate datasets, then confirm at the scale you care about.

courseTitle: Data-oriented design: struct-of-arrays vs array-of-structs
lessonTitle: SIMD lanes: contiguous loads, gathers, and blocked SoA
md: Vectorizing the instructions does not fix the layout. Vectorizing means rewriting a scalar loop, which handles one element per instruction, into SIMD instructions that handle 8 at once, and compilers can do it automatically. Even if a compiler vectorizes an AoS loop, the x values are still 12 bytes apart, so each register still needs a gather and the loop still pays for every unused byte in each line.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Keep less: minimisation, retention schedules and legal holds
md: Collect only what the purpose needs, give every record type a retention period and a trigger, enforce it with a job (not a policy document), and make legal holds the only thing that stops the job.

courseTitle: Data security: classification, DLP, databases and insider risk
lessonTitle: Insider risk: definitions, the Tesla files and running a programme
md: Insiders already have access, so the programme rests on context (HR events, role), behaviour against the person's own baseline, and exfiltration routes, combined as sequences. Build it with HR, legal and privacy from the start, and pseudonymise until there is cause.

courseTitle: Deception: honeypots, honeytokens and canaries
lessonTitle: Honeytokens and canary tokens: data that phones home
md: A hosted token service sees your alerts: the alert, including the triggering address, goes to whoever runs the token server. For sensitive placements, run your own. Thinkst publishes the Canarytokens server as open source and recommends its Docker image for self-hosting.

courseTitle: Deterministic inference: bitwise equivalence and reproducibility
lessonTitle: Two orderings, two answers: float addition is not associative
md: Floating-point addition is commutative but not associative. Reordering a sum is not a refactor, it is a different computation. Every other idea in this course follows from that sentence.

courseTitle: DevSecOps: CI/CD pipelines, infrastructure as code and policy as code
lessonTitle: DevSecOps: security checks on the path from commit to cloud
md: The pipeline is a privileged identity. Its definition files, its runners, its credentials and its state files deserve the same protection as production, because each one is a path into production.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Why generate text in any order other than left to right?
md: A diffusion language model keeps the Transformer and the maximum-likelihood goal of a GPT. It changes two things: attention is bidirectional, and generation fills in many masked positions per step in any order instead of one token at the end.

courseTitle: Diffusion language models: generating text by unmasking
lessonTitle: Making diffusion LMs useful: AR initialization, RL and remasking
md: The mechanism of a diffusion LM is unchanged by all three ideas. AR initialization reuses weights through the shift operation, RL and DPO replace the exact log-probability with cheap or variance-reduced estimates of the bound, and ReMDM changes only the sampler so that more steps can fix mistakes.

courseTitle: Disaggregated prefill and decode
lessonTitle: Chunked prefill or disaggregation: when each one wins
md: Disaggregation adds failure modes. DistServe notes a fault in one decode instance that serves several prefill instances can spread, and FCFS prefill can create a convoy effect where long prompts block short ones. Mooncake must sometimes reject a request after its prefill if no decode slot is left, wasting that prefill.

courseTitle: Disk, file system and mobile forensics
lessonTitle: Shortcuts, Jump Lists, ShellBags and the Recycle Bin
md: These artefacts show that a *user account* interacted with a file, a folder or a drive. They are strongest together and with the drive in hand.

courseTitle: DiskANN and CAGRA: billion-scale ANN on SSDs and GPUs
lessonTitle: DiskANN search: beam width, SSD reads and re-ranking
md: Beam width W trades round trips for wasted reads; search list L trades reads for recall. Tune L for the recall target first, then pick the smallest W that meets the latency target, watching total reads against the SSD's IOPS budget.

courseTitle: DPO and its variants: preference tuning without RL
lessonTitle: KTO: aligning with thumbs up and thumbs down, no pairs
md: Turning a pair into one desirable and one undesirable example, as the paper does to compare against DPO, is described by its authors as a naive assumption: a chosen answer is only better than its sibling, not necessarily good.

courseTitle: Online data migration (dual-write and backfill)
lessonTitle: Proving the new read path before trusting it
md: Not every mismatch is a bug in the new store. If the new store is fed asynchronously, from a queue or a CDC stream, it is eventually consistent with the old one: a read right after a write can compare a fresh control with a candidate that is milliseconds behind. Measure that lag, and only `ignore` such cases after confirming they converge.

courseTitle: eBPF tracing with bpftrace: probes, verifier, maps
lessonTitle: Overhead, pitfalls and using bpftrace in production
md: Common misconception: "eBPF is safe, so tracing can't hurt production." The verifier guarantees the kernel won't crash or hang, but it does not bound *how often* your program runs. A kprobe on a function called millions of times per second can still cost a large fraction of every CPU.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Why appliances are hard to defend: patches, logs and trust
md: Treat an appliance as a server you cannot see into. Get its logs out as they are written, limit the secrets it holds, and plan in advance for the day you must rebuild it.

courseTitle: Edge devices and exposure management: VPNs, firewalls and appliances
lessonTitle: Detecting a compromised appliance from the outside
md: When you cannot see inside a device, watch its edges: every connection it starts, every session that changes address, every account that uses it, and every configuration change. Those records live on other systems the intruder does not control.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Length penalties inside RL: Kimi k1.5 and DAPO
md: A length term changes which correct answers GRPO reinforces most. Without it, all correct answers in a group are equal; with it, the shortest correct one gets the largest advantage.

courseTitle: Efficient reasoning: overthinking and length control
lessonTitle: Whether to think at all: NoThinking, hybrid modes and routing
md: Deciding whether to think is often a bigger lever than shortening the thinking. Evaluate every option, from NoThinking to full thinking, on an accuracy-versus-tokens frontier per difficulty level, and check whether accuracy differences exceed the noise of your test set.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: Case mapping and case folding: when lower() is not one-to-one
md: Locale-aware case mapping makes it worse: in Turkish, `I` lower-cases to dotless ı. Code that lower-cases with the server's locale can give different answers on different machines. For identifiers, use locale-independent case folding, as Python's `str.casefold()` is.

courseTitle: Encodings, parsers and Unicode attacks
lessonTitle: Polyglot files, content sniffing and LangSec
md: Checking the first bytes of an upload is not validation. A file can carry one format's signature and another format's content. If a file must be an image, decode it with an image library and re-encode it to a fresh file; whatever was hidden in it does not survive.

courseTitle: How EDR works: telemetry, ETW, Sysmon and endpoint hardening
lessonTitle: Application control I: allowlisting and AppLocker
md: Microsoft states AppLocker is "a defense-in-depth security feature and not considered a defensible Windows security feature": it does not meet Microsoft's servicing criteria, so a bypass is not treated as a vulnerability. Use it to raise the bar and to control what users run; use App Control for Business where you need a security boundary.

courseTitle: Energy disaggregation (NILM): from Hart's edges to seq2point
lessonTitle: Hart's NALM: steady states, step changes and signatures
md: Event-based methods need step changes. Hart's own NALM page lists three appliance classes: ON/OFF (bulbs, toasters), multi-state (washing machines, dishwashers with fill, rinse and spin states) and continuously variable (light dimmers, variable-speed tools). The last class is hard to monitor nonintrusively because it does not generate step changes in power.

courseTitle: Entity normalization: job titles, schools and companies
lessonTitle: Scoring pairs with Fellegi-Sunter match weights
md: The independence assumption double-counts correlated fields. Company name and website domain usually agree or disagree together, so adding both full weights overstates the evidence. Merge strongly correlated fields into one comparison, or check calibration on labeled pairs: whether pairs scored 0.9 really match about 90% of the time.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Who runs the tenant: Entra roles, Global Administrator and PIM
md: Count who can become Global Administrator, not only who is one: role assigners, admin credential resetters, app credential managers and hybrid identity admins. Keep the count small, make it eligible rather than active, and keep two tested emergency accounts outside it.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Entra tokens: lifetimes, refresh tokens and revocation
md: Entra access is a chain: a 60 to 90 minute access token renewed by a 90-day refresh token that is bound to user and client, not to a resource. Revocation cuts the chain; CAE cuts the current link at Exchange, SharePoint, Teams and Graph.

courseTitle: Microsoft Entra ID and Microsoft 365 security
lessonTitle: Conditional Access in Entra: baselines and the gaps attackers use
md: A Conditional Access policy set is only as strong as what it does not cover. Inventory the exclusions, the service principals and the allowed flows, block legacy authentication and device code, and test every change in report-only mode first.

courseTitle: epoll and event loops: serving many sockets from one thread
lessonTitle: Why one thread per connection stops scaling
md: **Readiness notification**: you give the kernel a set of file descriptors and it tells you which ones can do I/O right now without blocking. You still perform the `read` or `write` yourself. An **event loop** is a thread that repeatedly waits for readiness, then runs a short handler (a *callback*) for each ready descriptor.

courseTitle: Avoiding overfitting to a public query set
lessonTitle: Adaptive overfitting: how score feedback leaks the test set
md: Do not read those results as "test reuse is safe." ImageNet's test set has tens of thousands of images and Kaggle private splits often thousands of rows. Search teams often tune against 50 to 200 queries with free-form changes (prompts, thresholds, filters). That is exactly the small-n, many-k regime where the toy overfits.

courseTitle: Exploit mitigations: ASLR, DEP, canaries and CFI
lessonTitle: From bug to control: why exploit mitigations exist
md: Common misconception: "the binary has every mitigation enabled, so this overflow is not a security issue." Every mitigation in this course has a known bypass class (lesson 14), and real exploits combine several bugs to get past them. An overflow is a security bug whether or not today's exploit techniques reach it.

courseTitle: False sharing and cache-line padding
lessonTitle: Four independent counters that refuse to scale
md: Correct code can still have false sharing. Tests pass, there is no race for a sanitizer (a race detector such as ThreadSanitizer, which flags conflicting unsynchronized accesses to the same memory) to report, and the profile only shows a slow, innocent-looking loop. It is found by measuring, not by reading for bugs.

courseTitle: Federated learning: training without moving the data
lessonTitle: Non-IID data and client drift: fast convergence to the wrong answer
md: On our toy problem, a proximal term with $\mu = 2$ moves the $E = 5$ fixed point from 1.944 to 1.995 and slows the first round from 1.320 to 0.988. It buys accuracy with speed, and it does not reach 2.3. Treat these methods as damping on drift, not as a cure; the honest cure for this toy is $E = 1$ or a control-variate correction.

courseTitle: Fine-grained MoE, shared experts, aux-loss-free load balancing
lessonTitle: From one MLP to many routed experts
md: Separate two numbers for every MoE model: **total parameters** (all experts, what you store) and **activated parameters** (what one token actually uses, which sets FLOPs per token). DeepSeek-V3 has 671B total and 37B activated per token.

courseTitle: FlashAttention-3 and FlashAttention-4
lessonTitle: FlashAttention-4 backward, scheduling, and using the kernels
md: Each generation chases the bottleneck the previous hardware exposed. FlashAttention removed HBM traffic for $S$ and $P$. FlashAttention-2 fixed work partitioning. FlashAttention-3 used Hopper's asynchrony to hide softmax and loads under the matmuls. FlashAttention-4 attacks the exponential unit and shared memory bandwidth, which stopped scaling with Blackwell's tensor cores.

courseTitle: Flow matching and rectified flow
lessonTitle: Sampling with Euler steps: why curved paths need more steps
md: Sampling cost is set by how curved the learned paths are. A perfectly straight, constant-speed flow is solved exactly by one Euler step.

courseTitle: Formal verification of systems code (TLA+, Verus)
lessonTitle: Verus: proving Rust functions with requires, ensures and invariants
md: Writing the invariant as `idx < n` looks natural but is wrong twice. Verus reports "invariant not satisfied before loop" (n can be 0) and "invariant not satisfied at end of loop body" (the last iteration makes idx == n).

courseTitle: FP8 and FP4 training: E4M3, scaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
lessonTitle: Scaling factors: sliding a tensor into FP8's window
md: The scale is a full-precision real number kept outside the FP8 data (in FP32), not a change to the format's exponent bias. The FP8 paper chose this deliberately: a software scale can take any value, while a programmable bias could only shift by powers of two.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust and safety: what these teams defend
md: Do not call it "just a business problem". Account takeover, scraping and carding cause data breaches and regulatory fines (you will see a EUR 265 million one in lesson 4), and the same signals and models also stop intrusions. Most fraud teams sit with, or next to, security.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Behaviour and velocity: counting what happens over time
md: Before a behavioural rule blocks anyone, test it against users of assistive technology and password managers. "Typed too fast" and "never moved the mouse" describe many legitimate users.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Card payments from zero: who is who, and where fraud lands
md: The issuer approves, the network sets the rules, and for card-not-present fraud the merchant usually pays when the cardholder disputes, unless the payment was strongly authenticated.

courseTitle: Fraud, abuse and trust-and-safety engineering
lessonTitle: Measuring it: precision, recall, friction and the missing labels
md: Choose thresholds by total cost, not by precision or recall alone. Wait for labels to mature, and keep a small random holdout, because blocked events never tell you whether they were fraud.

courseTitle: fsync, write-ahead logs and group commit
lessonTitle: The write-ahead rule: flush the log first, pages later
md: The write-ahead rule, in PostgreSQL's words: changes to data files must be written only after the log records describing them have been flushed to permanent storage. A commit is durable once its commit record is flushed; data pages can be written much later.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Seeds, dictionaries and corpus minimisation
md: Seeds change results more than people expect. Klees et al. (lesson 9) found that AFLFast, an AFL variant that changes which corpus entries get the most fuzzing, produced over 1,000 crashing inputs on `nm` from an empty seed but only 24 from a small valid seed, statistically the same as AFL's 23. Always report which seeds you used.

courseTitle: Fuzzing and vulnerability research
lessonTitle: Symbolic and concolic execution: solving for the input
md: Symbolic execution turns 'find an input that reaches here' into a math problem: collect the path condition, give it to an SMT solver, get a concrete input. Concolic execution keeps one foot in real execution to stay practical.

courseTitle: Fuzzy matching and string similarity
lessonTitle: Jaro-Winkler, trigrams and token scorers on the same pairs
md: `partial_ratio` produces false positives on short strings: `fuzz.partial_ratio("ai", "said hello")` is 100 because `ai` appears inside `said`. Likewise `token_set_ratio` returns 100 for any subset, so `google` vs `google cloud platform team` is a perfect score. Use these scorers with a minimum length or combine them with other evidence.

courseTitle: Geometric hashing and star-pattern plate solving
lessonTitle: Verification: accepting a match only when the odds reach a billion
md: The verification math assumes stray detections are independent and uniform. Satellite trails, diffraction spikes (the straight rays that bright stars show because light bends around the supports holding the telescope's secondary mirror), plate scratches and dense clusters violate that, so false positives there are far more common than the formula predicts. Mask streaks before solving.

courseTitle: Geospatial indexing and geo filters
lessonTitle: Better cells on the sphere: S2 cubes and H3 hexagons
md: All three systems are the same idea as lesson 3: name cells with integers, cover the query with cells, read those cells, then refine. S2 and H3 trade geohash's simplicity for cells that behave well everywhere on the sphere, including poles and the antimeridian.

courseTitle: GPU memory allocators and suballocation
lessonTitle: Best fit, splitting and merging inside segments
md: Misconception: "OOM with lots of reserved memory means a leak." Often it is fragmentation: the free memory exists but in holes smaller than the request, inside segments that cannot be released because a live tensor still occupies part of them.

courseTitle: GPU memory hierarchy and coalescing
lessonTitle: How a warp's 32 addresses become 32-byte sectors
md: **Misconception:** coalescing requires thread k to read element k. It does not. The Programming Guide notes that permuted access within the same 32-byte segments is just as good. What matters is the ratio of bytes used to bytes transferred.

courseTitle: GPU profiling and speed-of-light analysis with Nsight
lessonTitle: Timeline first: where the 14.52 ms actually goes
md: Remember the order. The timeline sets the denominator for everything else: a kernel that is 4 percent of the wall time can never give you more than 4 percent, however bad its counters look.

courseTitle: CUDA and Metal programming model: threads, blocks, warps
lessonTitle: Warps and SIMT: 32 threads, one instruction, and divergence
md: SIMT is not the same as SIMD. In CPU SIMD one instruction works on several values packed into one wide vector register (8 floats in a 256-bit AVX register, for example), and the software sees the vector width and manages lanes itself. In SIMT you write scalar per-thread code and the hardware groups it. Correctness never depends on warps; performance does, much like cache lines.

courseTitle: GraphRAG: entity graphs, communities, and global search
lessonTitle: Community summaries and map-reduce global search
md: Global search is not cheap per query. The docs call it resource-intensive: the map step makes one LLM call per batch of reports, so lower (more detailed) levels cost more calls. Picking the community level is a quality versus cost dial.

courseTitle: GRPO and RLVR: RL with verifiable rewards
lessonTitle: Why PPO is costly for LLMs and what GRPO removes
md: GRPO removes the **critic**, not the reward. In DeepSeekMath, GRPO was trained against a learned reward model. Rule-based verifiable rewards came to the fore with DeepSeek-R1. GRPO and RLVR are separate ideas that work well together.

courseTitle: Transit feeds: GTFS Schedule and GTFS Realtime
lessonTitle: GTFS Realtime messages and decoding them in Python
md: With FULL_DATASET, each fetch is the entire current state. If a trip's update was in the last message but is missing from this one, the consumer must treat it as having no realtime data now, and the reference is explicit that no TripUpdate does **not** mean the trip is on time.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: Kevin Mitnick: social engineering and the longest sentence of its day
md: "We'll train staff not to be fooled" is a weak defence on its own: a skilled caller is persuasive and polite, and the help desk is measured on speed. Build the process so that even a fooled agent cannot complete a reset without the out-of-band check.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: 2010: Operation Aurora and Stuxnet bring state operations into view
md: Aurora showed that a perimeter fails the moment one inside device is compromised, which led to per-request, device-aware access (zero trust). Stuxnet showed that code can break machines and that isolated networks are reached by people carrying media.

courseTitle: A history of hacking: landmark incidents and what they changed
lessonTitle: What the incidents changed: laws, institutions and safer defaults
md: Incidents changed security through four channels: law, institutions, defaults and architecture. Defaults and architecture protect people who never read a bulletin, so they matter most. When you meet a new incident, ask the five questions, then ask which of the four channels should change.

courseTitle: Side channels and hardware security
lessonTitle: Out-of-order and speculative execution, from zero
md: Speculation is safe for *results* and unsafe for *secrets*. The CPU guarantees that mispredicted work never changes what a program computes, but it was never designed to hide that the work happened. Every attack in lessons 7 to 11 is a way to steer transient instructions and then read their footprint.

courseTitle: HTTP request smuggling and web cache attacks
lessonTitle: CL.TE and TE.CL: two parsers, one stream
md: A desync needs only this: one hop reads **fewer** body bytes than the hop in front of it. The bytes it did not read become the start of the next request on that connection. Reject ambiguous framing at every hop and close the connection whenever framing is in doubt.

courseTitle: HTTP request smuggling and web cache attacks
lessonTitle: Web cache deception: making the cache keep a private page
md: Defence in depth matters here because the origin and the cache are often owned by different teams. The origin team should mark every personalised response `Cache-Control: no-store, private`; the CDN team should make sure no rule overrides that. Either alone has been bypassed in practice.

courseTitle: Huge pages: 2 MiB and 1 GiB mappings, hugetlbfs and THP
lessonTitle: Transparent Huge Pages: faults, khugepaged and memory bloat
md: `enabled=madvise` turns THP into an opt-in: only regions the application marks with `madvise(MADV_HUGEPAGE)` get huge pages at fault time. The THP doc recommends it where wasted memory matters, and `madvise(MADV_COLLAPSE)` (Linux 6.1+) lets a program request a synchronous collapse of a range.

courseTitle: Hybrid attention and SSM models
lessonTitle: Choosing the ratio and placement, and where hybrids still fall short
md: Known weak spots from the NVIDIA study: the 16K and 32K hybrids trailed the Transformer by about 1 point on long-context tasks, mostly multi-document QA where distractor passages may confuse the SSM state. Hybrids were also more prompt-sensitive: on MuSiQue the hybrid ranged 10.63 to 16.16 across prompt tweaks vs 15.25 to 17.68 for the Transformer.

courseTitle: HyDE: retrieving with a hypothetical document
lessonTitle: Worked toy: how averaging fake answers changes the ranking
md: Averaging fixes errors that differ from sample to sample. It cannot fix an error every sample shares, such as the LLM misunderstanding an ambiguous or unfamiliar query. That is the root of HyDE's main failure mode in lesson 5.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: DNP3, S7comm and OPC UA: from no security to secure by design
md: Secure protocols only help when they are on. An OPC UA server left in mode None, a DNP3 outstation without SAv5 keys, or a Modbus/TCP Security device that also listens on plain port 502 gives the attacker the old, unauthenticated path.

courseTitle: Industrial control system and OT security
lessonTitle: Incident response in OT: safety first, then manual
md: Two IT reflexes can hurt in OT: rebooting or reimaging a running HMI or server (NIST: rebooting 'may not be acceptable'), and running active scans across the control network during an incident. Both can stop the process or the operators' only view of it.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: XML signature wrapping: the verifier and the app read different parts
md: One parse, one element. The code that verifies the signature must hand the verified element to the code that makes decisions, and nothing else in the document may be consulted. Any second search of the document, by name, by position or by a second parser, reopens the gap.

courseTitle: SSO and federation: SAML, OIDC, SCIM and Golden SAML
lessonTitle: Detecting forged federation tokens and recovering trust
md: Resetting passwords, re-enrolling MFA or rebuilding one server does not remove a forged-token capability. Until the signing key is replaced everywhere it is trusted and the attacker's access is gone, the actor can mint a fresh login whenever they like.

courseTitle: Identity governance and privileged access management
lessonTitle: Separation of duties: toxic combinations and two-person control
md: Separation of duties makes misuse require collusion. Write the conflicting pairs down, check requests against them (preventive), scan existing access (detective), and add a mitigating control wherever a split is impossible.

courseTitle: Image alignment (homography) and change detection
lessonTitle: Solving for a homography with the DLT, by hand
md: A homography maps points only after dividing by the third coordinate. Code that multiplies by H and keeps the first two entries silently computes the wrong point everywhere except where W happens to be 1.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: The IR lifecycle: NIST 800-61r3, CSF 2.0 and SANS PICERL
md: Rev. 3's main shift is not new phases but a new framing: IR is part of everyday cybersecurity risk management, and improvement is continuous rather than a meeting at the end.

courseTitle: Incident response and digital forensics
lessonTitle: Memory forensics: processes, connections and injected code
md: Memory answers "what is running right now and talking to whom", which disk forensics cannot. That is why memory is captured first and why rebooting a suspect machine before capture is so costly.

courseTitle: Injection: when data becomes code
lessonTitle: SQL injection step by step: watching the query change
md: Removing the word OR, or blocking the quote character, is not a fix. It breaks real users (O'Brien, a shop in Portland OR) and misses inputs that need neither, such as a numeric field (lesson 6). The fix is to stop building SQL text out of input.

courseTitle: io_uring: asynchronous I/O through shared rings
lessonTitle: Submitting, waiting and how the kernel runs a request
md: Completions can arrive in **any order**. The ring preserves the order in which requests are *attempted*, not the order in which they *finish*. Always identify a CQE by its `user_data` (often a pointer to your per-request state), never by its position.

courseTitle: IoT and embedded device security
lessonTitle: Debug ports: UART, JTAG and SWD, and how makers lock them
md: Do not rely on hiding the pads (no labels, pins removed, epoxy). Those slow a curious owner and stop nobody determined. Treat physical obscurity as a delay, and make the chip itself refuse: burned debug fuses, disabled ROM download modes, no console login.

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: One thread for every request: how Node.js runs JavaScript
md: Node.js runs all JavaScript for all users on one Event Loop in one process with the user's full privileges. That gives JavaScript servers two bug classes that matter more than elsewhere: input that blocks the loop (denial of service for everyone) and input that changes shared objects (a change that persists for every later request).

courseTitle: JavaScript and Node.js security
lessonTitle: child_process: shells, arguments and Windows batch files
md: Prefer `execFile` or `spawn` with an argument array and no shell; put `--` before user-supplied values; validate values against an allowlist of expected forms; never combine an array with `shell: true`; and on Windows treat every batch file call as a shell call.

courseTitle: jemalloc, mimalloc and tcmalloc internals
lessonTitle: mimalloc: three free lists per page
md: mimalloc replaces a per-thread cache with ownership: the thread that owns a page allocates and frees into it with plain loads and stores, and everyone else uses a per-page atomic list that the owner drains in batches.

courseTitle: Kernel autotuning and configuration search
lessonTitle: The knobs, and how fast the space grows
md: The search space is a product, so it grows exponentially in the number of knobs and linearly in the number of shapes you tune for. Any plan that says "just benchmark them all" has to survive that product.

courseTitle: Kernel bypass: driving NICs and NVMe from user space (DPDK, SPDK)
lessonTitle: Handing the device to user space: vfio-pci, BARs and DMA memory
md: No IOMMU, no safety. `uio_pci_generic`, `igb_uio` and VFIO's `enable_unsafe_noiommu_mode` let the device DMA to any physical address. A bug in the application then corrupts the kernel or other processes: the ixy authors report losing a filesystem to rogue DMA writes on a misconfigured server. DPDK recommends vfio-pci with the IOMMU enabled.

courseTitle: Kernel fusion: moving fewer bytes through HBM
lessonTitle: Epilogue fusion, fused softmax and FlashAttention
md: Epilogue fusion matters less than elementwise fusion for big GEMMs: the matmul is compute bound and dominates, so removing a 66 us kernel from a 947 us layer saves about 7 percent. It matters more for small or skinny matmuls, where the GEMM itself is short.

courseTitle: Knowledge distillation: teaching a small model with a big one
lessonTitle: Matching what the teacher computes inside: hints, attention, states
md: Feature losses need alignment that output losses do not: a projection or regressor when widths differ (FitNets, TinyBERT's W_h), a layer mapping when depths differ, and the same spatial grid or the same token positions. Output distillation needs none of this, only the same set of classes or the same vocabulary.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Sizing the KV cache of Llama 3 8B, and why it caps batch size
md: A common slip is to use `num_attention_heads` (32) instead of `num_key_value_heads` (8) for a GQA model like Llama 3. That overstates its cache by 4x.

courseTitle: KV cache compression and quantization
lessonTitle: Keeping fewer tokens: windows, attention sinks and heavy hitters
md: Accumulated sums favor older tokens, which have had more steps to collect attention. In the toy, every later token entered with a tiny sum and was evicted within a few steps of leaving the recent slots.

courseTitle: KV cache offloading: tiers, reload vs recompute, and eviction
lessonTitle: Finding a prefix across tiers, requests and engines
md: Offload tiers are a bigger prefix cache with the same keys. A hit is the longest contiguous prefix found across all tiers; everything after the first gap is prefill.

courseTitle: Clocks: Lamport, vector and hybrid logical clocks
lessonTitle: HLC in production: 64 bits, bounded c, and uncertainty
md: HLC gives causality-respecting timestamps that look like wall time and fit in 64 bits. It does not make clocks agree: systems that need real-time guarantees still have to assume a skew bound and either wait it out (Spanner) or retry within it (CockroachDB).

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Why reasoning in word tokens is a bottleneck
md: Misconception: Coconut does not shrink the model or skip layers. Each latent step is still a full forward pass through all layers. What it removes is the trip through the LM head, sampling and the embedding table between passes.

courseTitle: Latent reasoning: chain of continuous thought (Coconut)
lessonTitle: Why superposition works: continuous thoughts and graph reachability
md: Read the theorem for what it is: a construction showing a 2-layer model with continuous thoughts *can* solve reachability in D steps, using embeddings as wide as the vocabulary. It does not show that a pretrained LLM learns this on GSM8k, and the matching experiments are small models trained from scratch on graph tasks.

courseTitle: Learned indexes: replacing B-tree search with a fitted model
lessonTitle: The last mile and the Recursive Model Index
md: Do not read stage-0 output as a position. In the example it predicts 3.75 for key 1, which is at position 0. Stage 0 is graded only on whether it routes keys to leaves that can fit them, not on its own accuracy.

courseTitle: Learned sparse retrieval with SPLADE
lessonTitle: SPLADE v2, SPLADE++ and running it in production
md: Do not read the tokens as an explanation. Elastic's docs warn that expansion terms are learned associations, not synonyms, and that low-weight tokens carry information jointly, much like dimensions of a dense vector. A surprising token in a result is not by itself a bug.

courseTitle: Linear attention and Gated DeltaNet
lessonTitle: Dropping the softmax turns attention into an RNN
md: Linear attention is not a cheap approximation of softmax attention that converges to it. The exponential kernel has an infinite-dimensional feature map (Katharopoulos et al.), so any finite state is a different, weaker model. That gap is what the rest of this course is about.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Where things live: the Linux filesystem from a defender's view
md: A detail worth remembering for later: if a program's file is deleted while it is still running, `/proc/<pid>/exe` shows the original path with ` (deleted)` appended (`proc_pid_exe(5)`). Legitimate software rarely does this; a process running from a deleted file in `/tmp` is a classic sign of an intruder cleaning up after starting a tool.

courseTitle: Linux for security: users, permissions, processes and logs
lessonTitle: Packages and updates, and the xz-utils backdoor
md: Patching closes most known holes, so do it promptly and automatically where you can, and reboot when the kernel or core libraries change. Package signatures protect the path from repository to you; they cannot vouch for the people upstream.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: One host is a checklist, a fleet is a control loop
md: A baseline you apply once decays. Write it down, apply it with an idempotent tool on a schedule, scan for drift, and stream telemetry off every host. The rest of this course fills in each box of that loop.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: The Linux audit system: how a system call becomes a record
md: Audit records come from the kernel, not the program, and one event is several records sharing TIME:SERIAL. auid (the login uid) is set once at login and survives su and sudo, which is what lets you attribute root actions to a person.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Tetragon: filtering and enforcing inside the kernel
md: Tetragon filters in the kernel and can act there. Hook LSM functions such as security_file_permission rather than raw system call arguments, start in observe mode, and pair Sigkill with Override when the operation itself must not happen.

courseTitle: Linux fleet hardening and telemetry: CIS, auditd and eBPF
lessonTitle: Immutable OS images: rebuild instead of repair
md: Immutable does not mean uncompromisable. A remote bug still gives an attacker code execution in memory until the next reboot, and writable areas still persist. Keep runtime telemetry; immutability shrinks persistence, not intrusion.

courseTitle: Evaluating generated text: metrics, LLM judges and human preference
lessonTitle: Why open-ended output is hard to score
md: An evaluator is a measuring instrument. Before trusting any number it produces, check how often it agrees with careful human judgment on your task, at the level (single output or whole system) at which you will use it.

courseTitle: Guardrails for LLM applications
lessonTitle: Amazon Bedrock Guardrails: policies, strengths and grounding
md: Read the coverage notes, not just the feature list. Per the AWS docs, sensitive information filters do not mask PII the model writes into tool call arguments, and grounding checks on a streamed response (one sent to the user piece by piece as it is generated) may mark it irrelevant only after it has been streamed. A guardrail protects only the channels it actually inspects.

courseTitle: LLM inference systems and KV-cache memory management
lessonTitle: When the pool runs dry: admission control and preemption
md: Preemption is not free throughput. The optimistic policy's extra batch size is partly spent redoing prefills, and a preempted request's latency can jump by a full prefill plus queueing. Frequent preemption is a sign the pool is too small for the configured concurrency.

courseTitle: LLM prompting and structured output: from prompts to masked logits
lessonTitle: Validation, retries and the pitfalls of strict formats
md: Treat structured output as a contract with three checks: did it finish (stop reason), does it fit (schema, often enforced by the decoder), and is it right (your validators and evals, test sets of inputs with known good answers). Leave the model an honest way out, put reasoning before answers, and measure quality with and without the constraint.

courseTitle: Latency and cost tradeoffs for LLM reranking
lessonTitle: Anatomy of one rerank call: tokens in, tokens out, two phases
md: Misconception: "output is only 60 tokens, so it is negligible." For billing it is small. For latency it is not, because prefill reads thousands of tokens in parallel while decode produces tokens one step at a time.

courseTitle: LLM as reranker: pointwise, pairwise and listwise prompting
lessonTitle: Why use an LLM as the last-stage reranker
md: An LLM reranker is a prompt plus an aggregation rule. Pointwise, pairwise and listwise differ in what one call sees (1, 2 or a window of passages) and therefore in how many calls a ranking needs and how hard each call is.

courseTitle: Local feature matching: Harris, SIFT, ORB and RANSAC
lessonTitle: Why corners make good features: the Harris response
md: Harris is invariant to rotation (eigenvalues do not change when the image rotates) but **not to scale**. Zoom in on a corner enough and, inside a fixed 3x3 window, it looks like an edge. Lesson 2 fixes this.

courseTitle: Lock-free stacks and queues: Treiber, Michael-Scott, Vyukov
lessonTitle: Why a preempted lock holder stalls everyone
md: Lock-free means a stalled thread can never stop the others: some operation always completes. It does not promise that any particular thread finishes, and it does not promise speed under contention.

courseTitle: Log parsing and log analytics: templates instead of regex
lessonTitle: Why one regular expression per format does not scale
md: A common dodge: "I will write regexes only for the formats I care about and drop the rest." You cannot know in advance which format you will care about during the next incident, and the lines you dropped are exactly the rare error templates. Dropping them also silently biases every count you compute afterwards.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: What to log, source by source
md: Never write secrets into logs. The OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet lists data to exclude or mask: passwords, access tokens, session identifiers (hash them if you need to follow a session), encryption keys, connection strings and sensitive personal data. Logs are copied widely, so anything in them leaks widely.

courseTitle: Logging and detection engineering
lessonTitle: Tuning and allowlisting without blinding yourself
md: Every allowlist entry is a promise that this pattern will never be malicious. Prefer fields the attacker cannot set (exact path in a protected folder, code-signing publisher, asset group from your inventory) over fields they can (process name, command-line text, user agent, file name).

courseTitle: Long context: RoPE scaling, YaRN and Ring Attention
lessonTitle: YaRN: a per-frequency ramp plus attention temperature
md: YaRN = per-pair ramp on rotations $r = L/\lambda$ (keep fast pairs, fully interpolate slow ones, blend between) plus a logit temperature $\sqrt{1/t} = 0.1\ln s + 1$, all baked into the precomputed cos and sin tables.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: Universal Transformers: recurrence over depth with a halting rule
md: Dynamic halting is not free accuracy. It helped on bAbI and LAMBADA but slightly hurt translation, adds a ponder-cost hyperparameter, and makes different positions in a batch finish at different times.

courseTitle: Looped and recurrent-depth transformers
lessonTitle: When looping helps, when it hurts, and the design space
md: Looping buys **depth** (multi-step reasoning, using context), not **capacity** (memorized facts). Judge a looped model on reasoning tasks at matched FLOPs, not only on perplexity at matched parameters.

courseTitle: LoRA, QLoRA and parameter-efficient fine-tuning
lessonTitle: The wider PEFT family, and when LoRA falls short
md: Hu et al.'s footnote already warned that a small rank should not be expected to work for every task: if the target were a different language than pretraining, full fine-tuning (like LoRA with r equal to the model width) could win. Low intrinsic rank was measured on tasks that are close to what the model already knows.

courseTitle: Machine unlearning: removing data and knowledge from trained models
lessonTitle: Hidden, not gone: relearning, probing and quantization attacks
md: A model that passes forget-set benchmarks in full precision can fail them after an ordinary 4-bit conversion that a user applies for deployment. Any release that relies on unlearning should evaluate the quantized versions people will actually run.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: Quarantine and Gatekeeper: the first-launch check
md: Gatekeeper is a first-launch, quarantine-triggered check. Removing the attribute (`xattr -d`), fetching with `curl`, or running a script through `bash` or `osascript` means it is never asked. Treat a process tree of browser or chat app, then Terminal, then curl, then shell or osascript as a detection signal, not as something Gatekeeper already covered.

courseTitle: macOS security for defenders
lessonTitle: FileVault, secure boot and startup security
md: The SSV, SIP and FileVault protect each other. Apple notes the system will not let a user turn off the signed system volume while FileVault is on, because a tampered OS could capture the password at next boot. A baseline should require Full Security, SIP, SSV and FileVault together, and MDM should report any Mac that drops one.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Triage: hashes, magic bytes and strings
md: Strings lie by omission. Serious malware encrypts or encodes its strings and builds them at run time, so a short, clean strings list is not evidence of innocence. A file with almost no readable text at all is itself suspicious, as the packing lesson shows.

courseTitle: Malware and reverse engineering
lessonTitle: Packing, obfuscation and entropy
md: High entropy is a signal, not a verdict. Installers, compressed images in resources, and legitimately UPX-packed tools are high entropy too. Combine it with other signs: few imports, a writable and executable section, a raw size much smaller than the virtual size, or a section name that is not one of the usual ones.

courseTitle: Matryoshka embeddings: one vector, many sizes
lessonTitle: Storage math: dimensions times bytes per number
md: Savings multiply, but so do quality losses. Each step (fewer dims, fewer bits) costs some recall, and the costs compound. Measure recall on your own queries at the exact size and precision you plan to serve, then use a rerank stage (next lesson) to win most of it back.

courseTitle: Megatron-Core performance: TP, PP, CP, MoE, FP8 and MFU
lessonTitle: Context parallelism: balanced causal splits and the KV ring
md: CP splits every activation along the sequence. Megatron balances causal work by giving rank i chunks i and 2CP - 1 - i, and hides the KV ring when each GPU holds enough tokens: c at least 2(H_kv / H)(F / B).

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Virtual addresses, page tables and the DTB, walked by hand
md: If an entry's present bit is 0, the page is not in RAM: it may be in the page file, compressed, or never used. The data is then simply not in a raw image. Tools report such reads as invalid addresses or blank fields, and an absent value is not evidence that something did not exist.

courseTitle: Memory forensics
lessonTitle: Linux memory: banners, task lists, bash history and kernel checks
md: Linux images fail more often than Windows ones because of symbols. Before an incident, build or collect ISF files for the kernels you run (the volatility3-symbols project publishes some pre-generated ones), and record `uname -a` at collection so you know which banner to match. The `-u` (`--remote-isf-url`) option lets Volatility search an online ISF index; `--offline` stops all downloads.

courseTitle: Memory fragmentation: why freed memory stays used
lessonTitle: Placement policy: where a block goes decides what survives
md: "Fragmentation is solved" is not the lesson. The study covers eight single-threaded C and C++ programs from the 1990s, and the authors call for more work on unusual program behaviour. Long-running servers with phase changes, many threads and per-thread caches are exactly that kind of workload, as the next lesson shows.

courseTitle: Memory ordering (acquire/release, seq_cst) and the C++/Rust model
lessonTitle: From orderings to instructions: x86-64, ARM64, and choosing
md: `volatile` is not an ordering. In standard C++, volatile accesses are not atomic and do not order other memory, so they cannot be used for synchronization between threads. (MSVC, Microsoft's C++ compiler, gives volatile acquire/release semantics by default on x86 targets; that is a compiler extension, not the language.)

courseTitle: Memory reclamation: epochs, hazard pointers, RCU
lessonTitle: Choosing a scheme: read cost versus bounded garbage
md: Do not benchmark a reclamation scheme with one thread on an idle machine. The cost differences that matter, garbage growth under preemption and fence cost on long traversals, only appear with oversubscribed threads (more runnable threads than cores, so some are always preempted), update-heavy workloads and long data structures.

courseTitle: Memory safety bugs: overflows, use-after-free and friends
lessonTitle: Integer overflow and signedness: when the size math lies
md: Every allocation size and every length passed to memcpy should come from a computation that cannot overflow and a value that cannot be negative. When a size comes from a file or a packet, validate it against the real data first.

courseTitle: Metric learning and re-identification
lessonTitle: Batch hard: mining the hardest pairs inside a P x K batch
md: Batch hard needs K of at least 2, or there is no positive to take a max over. And because it always picks the extreme pair, label noise and outlier crops dominate the loss: Hermans and colleagues show such outliers in Market-1501 and MARS (a video-based re-ID dataset) in their supplementary material.

courseTitle: Microbenchmarking pitfalls: when the number lies
lessonTitle: Noise, repetitions and when a difference is real
